newsitem.title: USA: Revised rules urged for U.S. diplomats in China.
newsitem.headline: Revised rules urged for U.S. diplomats in China.

text.p: Security inspectors have urged the State Department to review relaxed rules governing U.S. diplomats' contacts in China as part of a suggested security clampdown at U.S. missions in the communist country.

The recommendations were made as early as January, before a disclosure that the FBI was investigating an alleged Chinese plan to influence U.S. politicians by distributing some $2 million in campaign funds through proxies.
China has denied any plan to subvert U.S. domestic politics either by buying influence or reaching into the Clinton White House through the Democratic Party's campaign fundraising effort.

The security oversight team's full report was classified and distributed on a strict "need-to-known basis," according to an unclassified summary made available by Defense Week, a Washington-based newsletter publishing an account of its own on Monday.

"The key finding of the security oversight inspection of Embassy China and its four consulates general is the lack of adequate security resources commensurate with the importance of U.S.-China relations," a January-dated summary of the oversight group's findings said.

The group from the Office of Security and Intelligence Oversight, an arm of the Inspector General's office, urged more resources be devoted in China to U.S. facilities for "sensitive operations" as well as for security personnel and data processing systems, the summary said.

It said a recently revised policy governing personal relationships between U.S. mission personnel and Chinese nationals "needs to be re-examined to strike the proper balance between individual freedoms and adequate security safeguards."
The summary did not spell out whether this meant a call for tighter U.S. rules or a further relaxation, but the context left scant doubt that new curbs were at issue.

The Office of the Inspector General, the department's in-house watchdog, declined repeated requests to clarify its recommendation on contacts with Chinese nationals or discuss other aspects of its inspection of the U.S. premises in China.

Prior to a major post-Cold War easing of rules in 1995, State Department employees were barred from unauthorized contacts with citizens of countries deemed to pose a "hostile human intelligence threat" to the United States, including China and members of the former Soviet bloc.
Under the old policy, even a casual conversation struck up by a Chinese person in a bus in Beijing about the weather or a soccer match had to be reported to an embassy security officer.

After the State Department relaxed its "contact reporting" policy in May, 1995, employees were free to have social relationships with nationals of any country. Instead of disclosing all such contacts, they were required only to report any suspected effort by a foreign entity to recruit them or any request for classified or sensitive information from a foreign national.

A spokesman for the State Department's bureau of diplomatic security, which implements security standards at overseas posts, said his office had not yet responded to the Inspector General's recommendations.

The Security and Intelligence Oversight office conducts regular inspections of U.S. embassies to gauge the threat from spies as well as from terrorists, mobs, criminals or other intrusions. It recommends specific ways to counter feared vulnerabilities.

As of last December, the U.S. embassy in Beijing employed 161 "direct hire" State Department employees in addition to representatives of at least seven other U.S. agencies and departments. A combined total of 62 State Department employees serve at the consultates in Chengdu, Guangzhou, Shanghai and Shenyang, the State Department said.
